title: Predictable Cost & Latency Simulator: Specification and Validation Checklist
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

Purpose:
This document specifies the Predictable Cost & Latency Simulator (PCLS): a company-standard lightweight simulator and validation checklist teams must use to estimate per-request latency distributions and token-unit costs for proposed runtime changes (model upgrades, quantization, batching, kernel selection, memory layouts, and routing policy changes) before any staged rollout. The simulator is intended to be conservative, reproducible, and fast enough to run in CI and preflight pipelines.

Scope:
- Applies to: model serving changes (new model versions, precision changes, KV-cache behavior), routing/policy changes that alter execution path (fallback variants, cross-region routing), and infra changes that affect scheduling or preemption behavior.
- Out of scope: long-running load testing at fleet scale (use the perf-lab harness for full-scale testing). PCLS is for per-config, workload-local predictions.

Definitions:
- p95-latency: 95th percentile end-to-end response time measured from request arrival at rwd-router to final token emission.
- unit-cost: blended per-token cost estimate including GPU execution token cost, memory/DRAM charge, and amortized network overhead for streaming tokens.
- sample-workload: an anonymized, non-PII prompt trace representing the target application workload.

Design goals:
1) Predictability: simulator inputs are explicit and versioned (model artifact id, kernel profile, sequence-length histogram, batch-policy).
2) Conservatism: when uncertain, prefer pessimistic estimates (higher latency, higher cost) with documented uncertainty bounds.
3) Reproducibility: run deterministically in CI with recorded seeds and explainable approximations.
4) Lightweight: complete in under 90 seconds for a typical sample-workload (1000 requests) on a single CI worker.

Architecture (textual diagram)
- Input layer: sample-workload plus config file containing model_variant, quantization_profile, batch_policy, routing_policy.
- Execution model: microkernel-profile lookup leads to a per-token execution estimate, which is fed into a batching simulator, a KV-cache hit/miss model, and then a network/serialize latency layer.
- Cost model: per-kernel token-cost plus amortized pre/post processing costs and memory delta charge.
- Output: latency distribution (p50/p90/p95/p99), cost per request, hotspot breakdown (GPU, batching delay, serialization, network), and CI-friendly artifacts (JSON report and CSV traces).

Required Inputs
- model_id: immutable artifact id used by rwd-runtime (string).
- kernel_profile: kernel timing table name and version (string).
- seq_length_histogram: sequence length distribution as list of length:frequency pairs (CSV or JSONL serialized as string).
- batch_policy: policy name and parameters (e.g., continuous, fixed-N, adaptive).
- kv_cache_profile: hit_rate estimate (0.0-1.0) and avg_kv_latency_ms.
- concurrency_pattern: arrival process (poisson|bursty|steady) and mean_rate.
- quantization: profile id (none|int8|nf4|mixed).

Validation Checklist (must-pass to proceed to canary)
1) Completeness: Simulator run completed and produced a JSON report in the expected schema.
2) SLO delta check: predicted p95 must not exceed baseline p95 by more than the allowed delta in the change request (default +15%).
3) Cost delta check: predicted unit-cost must not exceed baseline by more than the allowed delta (default +30% unless product approval is provided).
4) Regression hotspots: any component contributing 20% or more of the delta must have an owner and an action plan attached to the change ticket.
5) Uncertainty bounds: bootstrap on trace samples to produce 90% confidence intervals; if interval width exceeds 12% relative, annotate the run as 'high-variance' and require manual review.
6) Sensitivity scan: run three additional simulations with arrival rate +/-10% and kv_cache hit rate +/-0.1; differences should be within tolerances or explicitly documented.
7) Artifact storage: upload simulator JSON report to the perf-artifacts bucket path perf/pcls/{change_id}/{run_id}.json.

Example config (YAML-like sample)
change_id: R-2026-1130-batcher-tuning
model_id: redwood-3b-v2:2026-01-15
kernel_profile: amx-ops-v3
quantization: nf4-compact
batch_policy:
  name: adaptive
  max_batch_size: 64
  latency_target_ms: 35
kv_cache_profile:
  hit_rate: 0.78
  avg_kv_ms: 1.2
seq_length_histogram: |
  16, 0.55
  32, 0.30
  128, 0.10
  512, 0.05
concurrency_pattern:
  type: poisson
  mean_qps: 12

CLI and CI integration
- Local run example: pcls run --config config.yaml --workload traces/sample-app-1.json --output ./reports/report.json
- CI job snippet (GitHub Actions): check out repo, run tools/pcls/bin/pcls run with config and upload resulting report as an artifact.

Metrics and Reporting Format
Required fields in the JSON report (keys must exist; use empty arrays if no data):
- change_id, run_id, timestamp, model_id, kernel_profile, quantization, batch_policy.
- latencies: p50, p90, p95, p99 in milliseconds.
- unit_cost_usd (per request).
- breakdown: list of component delta strings (e.g., 'gpu: +6.1ms', 'batching-delay: +12.4ms').
- uncertainty: p95_ci_lower and p95_ci_upper recorded as numeric strings.
- artifacts: raw_trace_csv path and histogram_png path as strings.

Hotspot categories and remedial actions
- GPU-kernel: re-evaluate kernel selection or request investigation from kernel-ops.
- Batcher: tune adaptive settings, reduce max_batch_size, or change latency_target_ms.
- KV-cache: investigate eviction patterns, warmup strategies, or increase cache sizing.
- Serializer/network: consider switching to gRPC streaming, adjust chunk sizes, or tune serialization buffers.

Acceptance gates and rollouts
- Must pass simulator validations and be approved by the owning service SRE and the model owner.
- If SLO delta is between +10% and +15%, require a staged canary at 5% then 20% traffic with automatic rollback if observed p95 exceeds predicted by more than +5%.
- If cost delta is >= +20%, product finance must approve or provide an offset plan.

Ownership and responsibilities
- Document owner: engineering service owner (must be set in the change ticket).
- Simulation tool maintainer: perf-infra team (on-call contact: perfinfra@redwood.com).
- Kernel profile sources: kernel-ops team.
- Cost model steward: finance-engineering.

Appendix: example report snippet (flat representation)
- change_id: R-2026-1130-batcher-tuning
- run_id: pcls-20260203-001
- model_id: redwood-3b-v2:2026-01-15
- p50_ms: 18.2
- p90_ms: 31.7
- p95_ms: 39.8
- p99_ms: 62.1
- unit_cost_usd: 0.0034
- breakdown_items: ["gpu: +6.1ms", "batching-delay: +12.4ms", "serialize: +1.3ms"]

Related artifacts and references
- perf-lab/harness README (full-scale load testing).
- kernel-ops/profile-catalog (kernel_profile naming and versions).
- docs/routing-policies (fallback and variant routing definitions).

Frequently asked questions (short)
Q: When should I prefer perf-lab over PCLS?
A: Use perf-lab for cluster-level behaviors (preemption across tenants, multi-node sharding) or to validate autoscaling and prewarming policies at scale. PCLS is for fast, per-change estimates.

Q: How does PCLS treat streaming token emission?
A: Streaming is modeled as incremental serialization plus network overhead per token and amortized GPU kernel time. Teams should include realistic chunk sizes in seq_length_histogram.
